title: How teachers are remaking classrooms for the AI age
author: Daniel Nenni
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

Reuters’ “How teachers are remaking classrooms for the AI age” examines how American educators are responding to students’ growing use of artificial intelligence. Teachers are replacing some homework with classroom writing, oral examinations and practical activities that reveal students’ understanding. San Francisco teacher Tristen Chang uses oral assessments, while New York mathematics teacher Bobson Wong asks students to explain their preferred methods. Others are returning to handwritten work or using AI to adapt teaching materials. The article presents a central challenge: protecting independent thinking while preparing students to use an increasingly common technology responsibly. reuters.com

These changes suggest that education must place greater emphasis on the process of learning. A polished essay or correct answer offers limited evidence of understanding when software can produce it instantly. Asking students to explain decisions, defend interpretations and respond to unexpected questions makes their reasoning more visible. Such assessments can also help teachers identify confusion before it becomes a lasting obstacle.

However, redesigning assessment requires care. Oral examinations may disadvantage students who experience anxiety or need additional processing time. Handwritten tasks can create barriers for learners who depend on assistive technology. Effective classroom policies should therefore offer accessible ways for students to demonstrate knowledge while maintaining clear expectations about independent work.

AI literacy also deserves attention. Students need opportunities to question generated answers, check evidence, recognize uncertainty and explain when they have used automated assistance. These habits can make AI use more thoughtful and accountable.

The broader lesson is that teachers need support, time and shared guidance to redesign learning effectively. Schools should evaluate whether each activity builds knowledge, judgment and confidence. Successful adaptation will depend on preserving meaningful human interaction while choosing technology for specific educational purposes. The goal should remain students who can think independently, explain their reasoning clearly and use available tools with informed judgment.
